name: C#
description: Value vs reference types, async/await, LINQ, disposal and the .NET runtime behaviours behind them.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What C# is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is C#, and what is it mainly used for?
cards.answer: A general-purpose, statically typed, object-oriented language from Microsoft that runs on .NET. It is used for web back ends (ASP.NET Core), Windows desktop apps, cloud services, and games — it is the scripting language of the Unity engine.
cards.explanation: Modern .NET is open source and cross-platform: C# programs run on Windows, Linux and macOS. The language evolves quickly, regularly borrowing good ideas from functional languages (pattern matching, records, LINQ).

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — A tour of C#

cards.prompt: Who designed C#, and when?
cards.answer: Anders Hejlsberg's team at Microsoft, released with the .NET Framework in 2002 (announced in 2000). Hejlsberg later also led the design of TypeScript.
cards.explanation: C# began as Microsoft's answer to Java and the two still look alike. The original .NET Framework was Windows-only; the cross-platform rewrite (.NET Core, now just ".NET") arrived in 2016.

cards.prompt: How does C# code run?
cards.answer: The C# compiler turns source into Intermediate Language (IL) packaged in assemblies (`.dll`). At run time the .NET runtime (the CLR) JIT-compiles the IL to native machine code. `dotnet run` builds and runs a project in one step.
cards.explanation: This is the same split as Java's bytecode and JVM. .NET can also compile ahead of time to a native executable (Native AOT) for fast start-up and small deployments.

cards.prompt: What does a minimal modern C# program look like?
cards.answer: One line, using top-level statements (C# 9 and later): the compiler generates the `Main` method for you.
cards.explanation: Older code wraps this in `class Program { static void Main(string[] args) { ... } }`, which is still valid. `Console.WriteLine` writes a line to standard output; statements end with semicolons.

cards.prompt: What kind of language is C#: typing, memory and paradigms?
cards.answer: Statically and strongly typed, with local type inference (`var`). Memory is garbage collected. It is primarily object-oriented, with strong functional features: lambdas, LINQ queries, pattern matching and immutable records. `async`/`await` (which C# popularised) is built in.
cards.explanation: C# distinguishes value types (`struct`, stored inline) from reference types (`class`, stored on the heap) — a distinction that matters for performance and for how assignment copies data.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — The C# type system

cards.prompt: What are the `dotnet` CLI and NuGet?
cards.answer: `dotnet` is the command-line tool for creating, building, testing and running .NET projects (`dotnet new`, `dotnet build`, `dotnet test`). NuGet is .NET's package manager and registry; `dotnet add package` installs from it.
cards.explanation: Projects are described by `.csproj` files, which list target framework and package references. IDEs (Visual Studio, Rider, VS Code with C# Dev Kit) drive the same `dotnet` tooling underneath.

modules.name: Types, Memory & Disposal
modules.description: Structs, classes, boxing, nullable reference types and deterministic cleanup.

cards.prompt: `struct` vs `class` in C#
cards.answer: Structs are value types copied on assignment; classes are reference types where the reference is copied.

left.title: struct (value type)
points: Copied on assignment and when passed
Usually on the stack or inline in its owner
Great for small, immutable, short-lived data

right.title: class (reference type)
points: Reference copied; object lives on the heap
Right for identity, inheritance, larger state

cards.explanation: Guidance: make a struct only if it is small (~16 bytes or less), logically a single value, immutable and not boxed often. Mutable structs are a classic bug source because you mutate a copy without noticing.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Choosing between class and struct

cards.prompt: What is boxing, and where does it sneak in?
cards.answer: Boxing wraps a value type in a heap object so it can be treated as `object` or an interface. It appears in non-generic collections, `object` parameters (including `string.Format` and older `params object[]` APIs), and calling an interface method on a struct through the interface.
cards.explanation: Each box is an allocation plus a copy plus later GC pressure. Generics avoid it — `List<int>` stores ints inline while `ArrayList` boxes each one. Since C# 10, string interpolation uses interpolated string handlers that format value types without boxing. Constrained generic calls (`where T : IComparable<T>`) also avoid the box an `IComparable` parameter would cause.

cards.prompt: The GC handles memory. Why does `IDisposable` exist?
cards.answer: Because the GC only manages memory, and only nondeterministically. Files, sockets, DB connections, locks and native handles need releasing at a known moment — that is what `Dispose`, and the `using` statement that calls it, are for.
cards.explanation: Finalizers are a last-resort safety net: they run on a separate thread at an unknown time and delay collection by a full GC cycle. Implement the dispose pattern, prefer `using var`, and use `SafeHandle` rather than writing finalizers yourself.

cards.prompt: What do nullable reference types actually change at runtime?
cards.answer: Nothing. They are compile-time annotations plus flow analysis: `string?` may be null, `string` should not be, and the compiler warns where you violate it. The runtime representation is identical.
cards.explanation: Enable with `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`. The value is in the warnings, so treat them as errors in CI — half-enabled nullability gives false confidence. The `!` null-forgiving operator silences the compiler and should be rare and commented.

cards.prompt: What does `record` add over `class`?
cards.answer: Value-based equality, a generated `ToString`, deconstruction, and `with` expressions for non-destructive mutation. `record struct` does the same for value types.
cards.explanation: Records suit DTOs, messages and domain values where two instances with the same data should be equal. Use `init`-only setters to make them genuinely immutable; the equality is still shallow, so a record holding a `List<T>` compares by list reference.

modules.name: Async & LINQ
modules.description: The async state machine, deadlocks, deferred execution and the traps behind both.

cards.prompt: Why can this deadlock in a UI or classic ASP.NET app?
cards.answer: `.Result` blocks the thread that owns the synchronization context; the continuation after `await` needs that same context to resume, so both wait forever. Await all the way up, or use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code.
cards.explanation: By default a continuation is posted back to the captured context. Blocking that context on the task creates a cycle. The rule: never block on async code — `async` should propagate to the entry point. ASP.NET Core has no such context, but libraries still cannot assume that.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Async guidance: avoid sync over async

cards.prompt: Why is `async void` dangerous?
cards.answer: There is no Task to await or observe, so the caller cannot know when it finishes, and an exception is thrown on the synchronization context — typically crashing the process instead of surfacing as a faulted task.
cards.explanation: The single legitimate use is an event handler, whose signature demands `void`. Everywhere else return `Task` (or `ValueTask` for hot paths that usually complete synchronously) so failures and completion are observable.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.explanation: LINQ query operators are deferred — `Where` builds an iterator and executes only when enumerated, at which point it sees the current contents of the list. Call `.ToList()` to snapshot, and beware enumerating an expensive query twice by accident.

cards.prompt: `IEnumerable<T>` vs `IQueryable<T>`
cards.answer: IEnumerable runs the delegate in memory; IQueryable builds an expression tree a provider translates — typically into SQL.

left.title: IEnumerable<T>
points: Filters after data has been fetched

right.title: IQueryable<T>
points: LINQ to a provider (EF Core, etc.)
Filters translate into the WHERE clause
Unsupported expressions throw or fall back

cards.explanation: Casting an `IQueryable` to `IEnumerable` too early is a classic performance bug: the whole table is pulled into memory and filtered there. Watch for it whenever you call a custom method inside a query.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Client vs server evaluation

cards.prompt: How should a long-running async API support being cancelled?
cards.answer: Accept a `CancellationToken` parameter, pass it to every async call you make, and check `token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` around synchronous loops.
cards.explanation: Cancellation is cooperative — nothing forcibly aborts a task. A token that is accepted but never forwarded is worse than none, because callers believe cancellation works. `CancellationTokenSource` also provides timeouts via `CancelAfter`.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Cancellation in managed threads

cards.prompt: What problem do `Span<T>` and `Memory<T>` solve?
cards.answer: They give a type-safe, bounds-checked view over contiguous memory — arrays, stack buffers or unmanaged memory — so you can slice and parse without allocating substrings or copies.
cards.explanation: `Span<T>` is a ref struct: stack-only, so it cannot be stored in a field or captured by an async method. `Memory<T>` is the heap-storable equivalent for async paths. Together they eliminate most parsing allocations in hot code.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Memory and span usage guidelines

modules.name: Language Essentials
modules.description: Parameters, equality, pattern matching, delegates, generics variance and modern syntax.

cards.prompt: `ref` vs `out` vs `in` parameters
cards.answer: All three pass by reference. `ref` requires an initialised argument and allows reading and writing; `out` need not be initialised but must be assigned by the method; `in` is a read-only reference.

left.title: ref / out
points: `ref`: caller must initialise; callee may read and write
Both visible at the call site

right.title: in / by value
points: By value (default): a copy of the value or reference
Reassigning a by-value parameter is invisible to the caller

cards.explanation: Without a modifier, C# passes by value — for reference types, the reference is copied, exactly like Java. `out` powers the `TryParse` pattern (`if (int.TryParse(s, out var n))`). `in` avoids copying large structs but can cause hidden defensive copies unless the struct is `readonly`.

cards.prompt: What is lost when this rethrows?
cards.answer: `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to this line, so you lose where the error really happened. Use a bare `throw;` to rethrow with the original trace, or wrap it: `throw new OrderException("...", ex)` to add context while keeping the inner exception.
cards.explanation: Also avoid catching `Exception` just to log and rethrow at every layer — logs fill with duplicates. Catch where you can handle or add context; let everything else bubble to one top-level handler. Exception filters (`catch (HttpRequestException e) when (e.StatusCode == 404)`) avoid unwinding for cases you will not handle.

cards.prompt: What does this print?
cards.answer: False True True
cards.explanation: For classes, `==` is reference equality unless the type overloads it; `Equals` is virtual and may be overridden. Records generate value-based `Equals` and `==`. Strings overload `==` to compare contents. When overriding `Equals`, override `GetHashCode` too — the same contract as Java.

cards.prompt: What kinds of patterns can a C# switch expression use?
cards.answer: Type patterns (`Circle c`), property patterns (`{ Status: "open", Total: > 100 }`), positional patterns for deconstructable types (`(0, 0)`), relational and logical patterns (`>= 18 and < 65`, `not null`), list patterns (`[1, .., var last]`), and the discard `_`.
cards.explanation: Switch expressions warn when a closed set of cases is not exhausted and return a value, so they replace long if/else chains. `is not null` is the idiomatic null check — it cannot be hijacked by an overloaded `==` operator.

cards.prompt: What are delegates, `Func`/`Action`, and events?
cards.answer: A delegate is a type-safe function reference. `Func<T, TResult>` returns a value, `Action<T>` returns void, and `Predicate<T>` returns bool. An `event` is a delegate field that outside code can only subscribe to (`+=`) or unsubscribe from (`-=`), never invoke or overwrite.
cards.explanation: Event subscriptions keep the subscriber alive as long as the publisher lives — a common leak when a short-lived object subscribes to a long-lived one and never unsubscribes. Raise events with `Handler?.Invoke(this, args)` to avoid a null race.

cards.prompt: What is an extension method, and what is LINQ's relationship to them?
cards.answer: A static method in a static class whose first parameter is marked `this` (`public static bool IsBlank(this string s)`), callable as if it were an instance method. LINQ operators such as `Where` and `Select` are extension methods on `IEnumerable<T>`.
cards.explanation: Extension methods cannot access private members and are resolved statically at compile time, so they cannot be overridden. C# 14 extension members extend the idea to properties and static members. Keep them discoverable in a clearly named namespace.

cards.prompt: What do `out T` and `in T` mean on a generic interface?
cards.answer: `out T` makes the interface covariant — `IEnumerable<string>` can be used as `IEnumerable<object>` because T only comes out. `in T` makes it contravariant — `IComparer<object>` can be used as `IComparer<string>` because T only goes in.
cards.explanation: Variance applies only to interfaces and delegates, and only to reference types. `List<T>` is invariant because it both accepts and returns T. Arrays are unsafely covariant — assigning a `string[]` to `object[]` compiles, and storing an `int` in it throws at runtime.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Covariance and contravariance in generics

cards.prompt: `const` vs `readonly` (and `static readonly`)
cards.answer: `const` is a compile-time constant baked into every assembly that uses it; `readonly` is a field assigned once, at declaration or in the constructor, evaluated at runtime.

left.title: const
points: Changing it needs consumers to recompile

cards.explanation: Because const values are copied into consumers at compile time, changing a public const in a library does not affect callers until they recompile. Use `const` for true constants (mathematical, protocol numbers) and `static readonly` for everything else.

cards.prompt: What do primary constructors, collection expressions, `required` members and file-scoped namespaces add?
cards.answer: Primary constructors declare constructor parameters on the type itself (`class Service(ILogger log)`); collection expressions build collections with `[1, 2, ..others]`; `required` members force initialisation in object initialisers; and `namespace X;` saves a level of indentation for the whole file.
cards.explanation: Together with records, pattern matching and top-level statements, they strip much of the ceremony from C#. Note that primary-constructor parameters in classes are captured mutable variables, not readonly fields — assign them to a `readonly` field if that matters.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — What's new in C# 12

modules.name: The .NET Runtime & Ecosystem
modules.description: The CLR and GC, Task vs ValueTask, async streams, dependency injection lifetimes, EF Core and tooling.

cards.prompt: How does C# code become machine code?
cards.answer: The C# compiler (Roslyn) emits IL (intermediate language) into an assembly. At runtime the CLR JIT-compiles IL to native code per method on first call, with tiered compilation re-optimising hot methods. Native AOT compiles ahead of time instead.
cards.explanation: Tiered compilation plus dynamic PGO give fast startup and fast steady state. Native AOT trades reflection-heavy features for instant startup and small self-contained binaries — ideal for CLIs, containers and serverless.

cards.prompt: How does the .NET garbage collector organise the heap?
cards.answer: Into generations 0, 1 and 2, where short-lived objects die cheaply in gen 0, plus the large object heap (LOH) for objects of 85,000 bytes or more, which is collected with gen 2 and not compacted by default.
cards.explanation: Frequent large allocations — big arrays and strings — cause expensive gen 2 collections and LOH fragmentation. `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` and `Span<T>` reduce them. Server GC (the ASP.NET Core default) uses a heap per core for throughput; workstation GC favours latency.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Fundamentals of garbage collection

cards.prompt: `Task<T>` vs `ValueTask<T>`
cards.answer: Task is a reference type that is always allocated (except cached results); ValueTask is a struct that avoids allocation when the result is usually available synchronously.

left.title: Task<T>
points: Await it many times, store it, combine it
Safe default for every async API

right.title: ValueTask<T>
points: Struct — no allocation on the sync path
Hot paths that usually complete synchronously

cards.explanation: ValueTask is an optimisation for hot paths that usually complete synchronously, such as a cached read. It has rules: await it exactly once, never await it concurrently, and call `.AsTask()` if you need to store or reuse it. Default to `Task`.

cards.prompt: What is `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` for?
cards.answer: Streaming results that arrive asynchronously: the producer is an `async` iterator using `yield return`, and the consumer uses `await foreach`. Each item is awaited as it arrives instead of buffering the whole list.
cards.explanation: Use it for paging through APIs, reading database results, or processing message streams with bounded memory. Pass cancellation with `[EnumeratorCancellation]` on the token parameter, and `.WithCancellation(ct)` on the consuming side.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Generate and consume async streams

cards.prompt: This registration causes intermittent data corruption under load. Why?
cards.answer: A captive dependency: a singleton service captures a scoped `DbContext`, so one context — which is not thread-safe — is shared by every request forever. A service may depend only on services with equal or longer lifetimes. Make the consumer scoped, or inject `IServiceScopeFactory` and create a scope per operation.
cards.explanation: Lifetimes: transient (new every resolution), scoped (one per request), singleton (one for the app). ASP.NET Core validates scopes in Development and throws on this exact mistake — enable `ValidateScopes` and `ValidateOnBuild` everywhere, including tests.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Dependency injection — service lifetimes

cards.prompt: An EF Core list page runs 101 queries and is slow even with one query. What do you check?
cards.answer: N+1 from lazy loading or per-row navigation access — load related data with `Include` or project with `Select` into a DTO. For read-only pages add `AsNoTracking()` to skip change tracking. Log the generated SQL to see what actually runs.
cards.explanation: Projections (`Select(o => new OrderRow(o.Id, o.Customer.Name))`) fetch only needed columns and never track. Watch for client evaluation, cartesian explosion from several `Include`s (use `AsSplitQuery`), and calling `ToList()` too early, which moves filtering into memory.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — EF Core — efficient querying

cards.prompt: What do the `dotnet` CLI, NuGet and SDK-style projects give you?
cards.answer: One CLI for everything — `dotnet new`, `build`, `test`, `run`, `publish`, `format`. NuGet is the package registry, referenced by `<PackageReference>` in SDK-style `.csproj` files. `Directory.Packages.props` centralises versions across a solution.
cards.explanation: Enable `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`, `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>` and analyzers in CI. Use a lock file (`RestorePackagesWithLockFile`) for reproducible restores, and `global.json` to pin the SDK version the team builds with.

cards.prompt: How do xUnit tests differ from NUnit/MSTest, and what are `[Fact]` and `[Theory]`?
cards.answer: `[Fact]` is a test with no parameters; `[Theory]` with `[InlineData]` or `[MemberData]` runs one test over many inputs. xUnit creates a new class instance per test, so the constructor is setup and `IDisposable` is teardown — no shared mutable state by accident.
cards.explanation: Shared expensive setup goes in class or collection fixtures. For ASP.NET Core, `WebApplicationFactory<T>` runs the real app in memory for integration tests; Testcontainers provides real databases. The per-test instance model is the main philosophical difference from NUnit.
